bibliographic.title: Generative AI as interactional infrastructure for meaning-centered care in later life
bibliographic.citation_apa: Chen, B., & Jin, A.-Y. (2026). Generative AI as interactional infrastructure for meaning-centered care in later life. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 17, 1883962. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1883962

methodology.method_family: perspective article with conceptual framework synthesis
methodology.sector: mental health and public mental health for older adults
methodology.technology_context: GenAI and LLMs as conversational, multimodal digital mental health applications including chatbots, triage, clinical decision support, and AI-augmented psychological interventions in hospital and community care settings

eligibility.decision_rationale: Perspective article directly addressing GenAI/LLMs as conversational mental health infrastructure, explicit human-supervised bounded deployment, and a Governing layer with safeguards for privacy, hallucination, dependency, crisis escalation, and cultural adaptation in a regulated healthcare context for older adults.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only partial front-matter and early sections were provided; full framework operationalization, governance mechanisms, and limitations sections may extend beyond supplied text.

appraisal.notes: Deliberately conceptual perspective, not empirical study. Authors state they do not assume current LLMs are ready to conduct psychotherapy. Framework draws on meaning-centered psychotherapy, dignity therapy, life review, gerotranscendence theory, care ethics, and implementation science. Appropriate for theoretical contribution but weak on operational governance implementation detail in supplied text.

cerqual.explanation: Internally coherent conceptual framework with clear governance and human-supervision claims, but no empirical validation, deployment case, or detailed audit/monitoring protocols in the supplied text; confidence moderated by conceptual-only design.

coding.theme: Governance-oriented conceptual framing of conversational GenAI in regulated mental health for older adults

synthesis.main_claim: GenAI/LLMs should function as bounded, human-supervised interactional infrastructure for meaning-centered care in later life rather than as autonomous substitutes for clinicians, caregivers, or human presence.
synthesis.contribution: Proposes a Sensing-Narrating-Connecting-Governing framework that shifts evaluation from model performance toward existential well-being, dignity, continuity of self, therapeutic alliance, equity, workflow integration, and explicit safeguards.
synthesis.limitations: Conceptual rather than technological-determinist argument; authors do not assume current LLMs are ready to conduct psychotherapy or that multimodal sensing can infer meaning without human interpretation; supplied text does not provide empirical implementation or audit/tracing detail.
synthesis.use_in_review: Central conceptual evidence for governance-oriented conversational GenAI in regulated mental health, especially human supervision, escalation boundaries, and safeguard categories; useful for framework mapping but not for operational governance mechanisms or post-deployment monitoring practices.

evidence.claim: Article is a peer-reviewed journal perspective on GenAI and LLMs in mental health.
evidence.excerpt: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and large language models are rapidly entering mental health research and service delivery

evidence.claim: Study type is conceptual perspective, not empirical evaluation.
evidence.excerpt: This perspective argues that GenAI should not be conceptualized as an autonomous substitute for clinicians, nurses, social workers, or family caregivers.

evidence.claim: Authors propose a four-layer governance-inclusive framework.
Framework includes explicit operational safeguards relevant to conversational AI governance.
evidence.excerpt: operate under explicit safeguards for privacy, hallucination, dependency, crisis escalation, and cultural adaptation.

evidence.claim: Deployment must be bounded and human-supervised.
evidence.excerpt: GenAI may contribute to public mental health only when deployed as a bounded, human-supervised, culturally responsive layer of relational augmentation rather than as a replacement for human presence.

evidence.claim: Technology context includes conversational LLM applications.
evidence.excerpt: GenAI can produce conversational responses, summarize complex narratives, generate psychoeducational content, and integrate text, speech, image, and behavioral signals into interactive applications.

evidence.claim: Mental health chatbots and conversational systems are within scope.
evidence.excerpt: this has stimulated interest in chatbots, digital triage, clinical decision support, simulated patients, risk monitoring, and AI-augmented psychological interventions.

evidence.claim: Regulated healthcare context is present via hospital affiliations and public mental health framing.
evidence.excerpt: 1Third Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University, Wenzhou, China, 2Wenzhou Central Hospital, Wenzhou, China

evidence.claim: Authors reject autonomous psychotherapy use of current LLMs.
evidence.excerpt: We do not assume that current LLMs are ready to conduct psychotherapy, nor that multimodal sensing can infer meaning without human interpretation.

evidence.claim: Consumer-facing chatbot design is considered insufficient for regulated mental health use.
evidence.excerpt: it also demands stronger boundaries than ordinary consumer-facing chatbot design.

evidence.claim: Meaning-centered care cannot be reduced to empathic chatbot questioning alone.
evidence.excerpt: It is tempting to imagine that an empathic chatbot could deliver meaning-centered care simply by asking reflective questions. This would be a mistake.
evidence.section: Why meaning-centered care cannot be reduced to chatbot support

evidence.claim: Evaluation criteria extend beyond model performance to relational and ethical outcomes.
evidence.excerpt: The proposed framework shifts evaluation from model performance alone toward existential well-being, dignity, continuity of self, therapeutic alliance, equity, and workflow integration.
